name: Acute Cholecystitis

likely: Anaerobes (Bacteroides) — more relevant in severe/gangrenous cholecystitis
pathogens.why: Acute cholecystitis pathogens reflect the same enteric flora seen in other biliary tract infections, dominated by gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae, with anaerobes becoming more relevant in more severe, necrotizing presentations.

investigations.why: First-line imaging — gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid support the diagnosis.
Typically mildly elevated; significant jaundice should prompt consideration of choledocholithiasis or cholangitis instead.
Leukocytosis supports the diagnosis and tracks response.
May identify bacteremia and guide de-escalation.

reason: Right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy's sign and fever, in the absence of jaundice, is consistent with acute cholecystitis (typically calculous). Antibiotics should be started alongside surgical consultation for cholecystectomy (early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment in most cases) — antibiotics are an adjunct to, not a substitute for, source control.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Chap. 357 (Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts), pp. 2730-2734; acute abdomen differential/imaging, Chap. 16, pp. 113-115
clinicalPearls: Acute cholecystitis usually opens as an attack of biliary pain that progressively worsens and becomes more generalized in the right upper abdomen; pain may radiate to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder (Harrison 22e p.2732).
Roughly 60-70% of patients recall prior self-limited biliary attacks before the index episode of acute cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2732).
Biliary pain that persists beyond about 5 hours should raise suspicion of acute cholecystitis rather than uncomplicated biliary colic (Harrison 22e p.2731).
Fever or rigors accompanying biliary pain generally signal a complication such as cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2731).
Murphy's sign: deep inspiration or cough during subcostal palpation of the RUQ produces increased pain with inspiratory arrest, a characteristic bedside finding (Harrison 22e p.2732).
An enlarged, tense gallbladder is palpable in only about 25-50% of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2732).
Generalized peritoneal signs and abdominal rigidity are usually absent in uncomplicated acute cholecystitis; their presence should prompt concern for perforation (Harrison 22e p.2732).

About 75% of medically treated patients remit within 2-7 days, but roughly 25% develop a complication despite conservative management, and recurrence is common (about 25% within 1 year) (Harrison 22e p.2732).
In empyema or free perforation the picture may mimic cholangitis with high fever, severe RUQ pain, marked leukocytosis, and prostration (Harrison 22e p.2733).
A sudden transient relief of RUQ pain (gallbladder decompression) followed by generalized peritonitis suggests free perforation (Harrison 22e pp.2733-2734).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute cholecystitis is acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall that usually follows obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone. Three mechanisms drive the inflammatory response: mechanical inflammation from increased intraluminal pressure and distention producing mucosal/wall ischemia; chemical inflammation from release of lysolecithin (via phospholipase action on biliary lecithin) and other local tissue factors; and bacterial inflammation, which contributes in roughly 50-85% of cases. Chronic cholecystitis is almost always associated with gallstones and results from repeated bouts of subacute/acute inflammation or persistent mechanical irritation of the wall by stones (Harrison 22e pp.2732-2733).
additionalDifferentials: Choledocholithiasis / common bile duct stone (suggested by elevated bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase with biliary pain) (Harrison 22e p.2731)
Peptic ulcer disease, especially perforated peptic ulcer (Harrison 22e p.113, p.155)
Right lower-lobe pneumonia / pleurisy / subdiaphragmatic abscess (Harrison 22e p.113)
Mirizzi's syndrome (cystic-duct/gallbladder-neck stone compressing the CBD with obstruction and jaundice) (Harrison 22e p.2732)
infectionMimics: Acute cholangitis (overlapping fever, RUQ pain, leukocytosis; empyema of the gallbladder may clinically resemble cholangitis) (Harrison 22e p.2733)
Right-sided pneumonia / empyema / subdiaphragmatic abscess presenting as RUQ pain (Harrison 22e p.113)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute pancreatitis (HIDA scanning can help differentiate acute cholecystitis or biliary colic from acute pancreatitis; serum amylase may rise in cholecystitis as well) (Harrison 22e pp.114-115, p.155)
Uncomplicated biliary colic / symptomatic cholelithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2731)
Acalculous cholecystopathy (gallbladder dysmotility causing recurrent biliary-type RUQ pain without stones) (Harrison 22e p.2733)
Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction causing recurrent RUQ pain (Harrison 22e p.2733)
Myocardial infarction / pericarditis (epigastric/RUQ overlap in the acute abdomen differential) (Harrison 22e p.113)
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound demonstrates calculi in about 90-95% of cases and shows signs of inflammation: gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and bile-duct dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2732).

Radionuclide (HIDA/DISIDA) biliary scan can be confirmatory when bile-duct imaging is seen without gallbladder visualization, indicating cystic-duct obstruction; useful when ultrasound is equivocal (Harrison 22e p.2730, p.2732).
WBC count typically shows leukocytosis around 10,000-15,000/uL with a left shift (Harrison 22e p.2732).
Serum bilirubin is mildly elevated (<5 mg/dL [85.5 umol/L]) in fewer than half of patients; about one-fourth have modest aminotransferase elevations (usually <5-fold) (Harrison 22e p.2732).
CT or ultrasound showing a large, tense, static, stone-free gallbladder with poor emptying can support acalculous cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2733).

Plain abdominal film may reveal gas within the gallbladder lumen/wall or pericholecystic tissues in emphysematous cholecystitis, and pneumobilia in cholecystoenteric fistula/gallstone ileus (Harrison 22e p.2733).
redFlags: Generalized peritoneal signs / abdominal rigidity (suggests perforation) (Harrison 22e p.2732)

High fever, severe RUQ pain, marked leukocytosis, and prostration resembling cholangitis (suggests empyema of the gallbladder, which carries high risk of gram-negative sepsis and perforation) (Harrison 22e p.2733)
Gas in the gallbladder lumen/wall on imaging (emphysematous cholecystitis; considerable morbidity/mortality) (Harrison 22e p.2733)
Transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis (free perforation) (Harrison 22e pp.2733-2734)

Acute cholecystitis arising in the setting of severe critical illness (trauma, burns, prolonged fasting, major non-biliary surgery) suggesting acalculous disease with a higher complication rate (Harrison 22e p.2733)
harrison.prognosis: Most medically treated patients (about 75%) achieve remission of acute symptoms within 2-7 days, but roughly 25% develop a complication requiring prompt surgery. Among those who remit, about 25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years, so early surgery is preferred. Mortality for emergency cholecystectomy is about 1-3%, versus about 0.5% for early elective cholecystectomy in patients under 60, rising with age and comorbidity. Acalculous and emphysematous forms carry higher complication and mortality rates, and free perforation has a mortality of roughly 30% (Harrison 22e pp.2732-2734).
pitfalls: Vague post-fatty-meal symptoms (epigastric fullness, dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence) are nonspecific and should not be misread as biliary pain (Harrison 22e p.2731).
Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; when present it may reflect bile-duct involvement or a coexisting CBD stone rather than simple cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2732).
Leukocytosis alone should never be the single deciding factor for operation, and a normal WBC count does not exclude a surgical abdomen including perforation (Harrison 22e p.155).
Clinical features of acalculous cholecystitis are indistinguishable from calculous disease; diagnosis depends on recognizing the critically ill setting and using imaging (Harrison 22e p.2733).

Emphysematous cholecystitis presents essentially like nongaseous cholecystitis clinically and is identified by imaging, not by a distinct clinical picture; it favors elderly men and diabetics (Harrison 22e p.2733).

Acalculous cholecystitis can occur with unusual organisms (e.g., Leptospira, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae) or systemic disease, so failure to find stones at surgery does not exclude cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2733).
